subject: Banking
title: The Speed of Modern Failures
description: A quick, practical guide to The Speed of Modern Failures.

hook.text: In the 1930s, bank runs took weeks. Continental Illinois took days. SVB took hours. Speed is getting faster.

buildup.text: Digital banking lets depositors move billions instantly. There's no line at the door — just a button on a phone.

discovery.text: Social media amplifies panic. A single tweet can trigger $42 billion in withdrawals before regulators even respond.

twist.text: Regulators still operate at 1930s speed. By the time they hold a meeting, the bank is already gone.

climax.text: Technology made banking faster but also made failure faster.

punchline.text: Weeks to days to hours. Bank failures now happen at app speed.

quiz.question: How has technology changed bank failures?
options: Dramatically increased the speed of bank runs

details.summary: Modern bank failures happen at digital speed, with billions in deposits moving in hours rather than days. Social media-driven panics and mobile banking combine to compress what once took weeks into a matter of hours.
details.whyItMatters: The speed of modern failures outpaces regulators' ability to respond. Traditional intervention tools designed for a world of physical bank lines may be too slow for an era of viral tweets and instant mobile transfers.
takeaways: SVB lost $42 billion in a single day compared to days or weeks for older bank runs
Social media amplifies fear faster than any communication medium in history
Regulatory response frameworks were designed for a slower, pre-digital world

faq.question: Why are modern bank failures so much faster?
faq.answer: Mobile banking allows instant transfers without visiting a branch, social media spreads fear in minutes, and group chats allow coordinated withdrawals. What once required standing in line now happens with a few taps on a phone.

faq.question: How can regulators adapt to faster bank runs?
faq.answer: Proposed solutions include real-time monitoring of deposit flows, faster emergency lending mechanisms, social media surveillance for emerging panics, and potentially the ability to temporarily pause digital withdrawals during acute crises.
